title: A really awkward first date
author: Melissa Muth Martinez
summary: Muth Martinez argues that workplace communication breaks down most often when norms go undefined or unstated, comparing a team without shared norms to a first date where nobody has said what they want. She offers the PTR framework, Preferences, Traditions and Requirements, as a tool for naming what is happening. Preferences are personal and subjective, traditions are inherited and often unexamined, and requirements are the non-negotiables that give structure and equity. She admits a bias toward requirements but warns that many are arbitrary or top-down. The leader's job is to design environments where people can contribute despite their differences, knowing when to honour a preference, retire a tradition or document a new expectation. The piece is a compact, usable framework with a clear leadership target.
points: Communication norms that go undefined or unstated are the most problematic cause of breakdown, since people fill the gap with assumptions.
PTR separates what is merely preferred, what is simply inherited, and what is truly required, prompting a check on whom each practice serves.
Traditions are often unexamined and can quietly block better ways of working.
Well-designed requirements reduce ambiguity and friction and create a fairer playing field, but arbitrary top-down ones undermine trust.
Leadership is less about enforcing one communication style than about designing environments where different people can contribute.
quotes: The most problematic issue I would argue, however, is when communication norms go undefined, or worse, unstated.

Without clear communication norms, people make assumptions and, in some cases, go rogue. Someone on the team might assume an email needs a response within the hour, while another thinks a week is totally acceptable.
PTR, which stands for Preferences, Traditions, and Requirements, is a tool for alignment.

Preferences aren’t right or wrong, but they’re innately biased and subjective. So, understanding our preferences and those of others is vital to building empathy and reducing friction in our interactions.

Traditions can provide a sense of comfort and lore, but they’re often deep-seated and hard to break. Over time, traditions may be more inhibitive than anything else, blinding us from our ability to unearth a better way of doing things.
When designed with thoughtfulness and care, requirements can reduce ambiguity and friction, while creating a more equitable playing field where everyone understands what’s expected of them and why.
Leadership is less about enforcing a particular way of communicating and more about designing environments where people can show up and contribute despite their differences.
